titleEn: Through God we will do valiantly
progression: | D D | G G | D A | D D |
intro: Fourteen verses, and only the first of them is new. Verses 2 to 6 are the closing half of Psalm 57, verses 7 to 14 are the closing half of Psalm 60, and the three word heading at verse 1 replaces the two long headings those psalms carry. Nothing here needs to be learned twice: if you have worked through 57 and 60 you already have the vocabulary, and the exercise is different. Read this page for the seam. The two halves came from a song of confidence sung in hiding and a lament after a defeat, and putting them end to end produces a psalm that praises first and asks second, which is the reverse of both parents. The wording is not quite identical either, and the small differences are listed verse by verse below.

stichs.en: A song. A psalm of David.

verses.summary: The only line in the psalm without a parallel elsewhere. Three words, where Psalm 57 heads its text with a tune name and a cave and Psalm 60 with a tune name and a campaign.

stichs.en: My heart is steady, God,
let me sing and make music,
with my glory too.

verses.summary: Psalm 57:8 says my heart is steady twice; here it is said once. In exchange this verse ends with two words, {{2.5}} and {{2.6}}, that in Psalm 57 open the following verse as awake, my glory.

stichs.en: Awake, harp and lyre;
let me wake the dawn.

verses.summary: Five words against seven in Psalm 57:9, which wakes the glory first and then repeats the imperative for the instruments. Here there is one waking of instruments and then the dawn.

stichs.en: I will thank You among the peoples, LORD,
and sing to You among the nations.

glosses: and I will sing to You
verses.summary: Two changes from Psalm 57:10. The divine name at {{4.2}} is the four letter name where Psalm 57 has my Lord, and the second verb here carries a joining vav that Psalm 57 does not have.

stichs.en: For Your kindness is great, higher than the heavens,
and Your truth reaches the clouds.

verses.summary: The one difference here changes the sense. {{5.2}} means above or beyond; Psalm 57:11 has the shorter preposition meaning as far as. Kindness that reaches the sky becomes kindness that clears it.

stichs.en: Be exalted above heavens, God;
and over all the earth, Your glory.

verses.summary: The refrain that closes Psalm 57, reused here as a joint rather than an ending. The only difference is the vav at {{6.4}}, which turns two separate clauses into one sentence.

stichs.en: So that Your beloved may be rescued,
save with Your right hand and answer me.

verses.summary: The second source begins, word for word as Psalm 60:7. In Psalm 60 this plea follows five verses of accusation; here it follows praise, and the same sentence reads as trust rather than desperation.

stichs.en: God has spoken in His holiness: let me exult.
Let me parcel out Shechem and measure off the valley of Succoth.

verses.summary: Identical to Psalm 60:8. An old oracle quoted inside the psalm, in which the land is treated as an estate to be surveyed rather than a front line.

stichs.en: Gilead is mine, Manasseh is mine,
Ephraim is the stronghold on my head,
Judah is my commander's staff.

verses.summary: One letter apart from Psalm 60:9: the second mine at {{9.2}} has no joining vav here, where Psalm 60 has one. The list of holdings is otherwise the same, north then south.

stichs.en: Moab is my washbasin,
on Edom I fling my sandal,
over Philistia I shout in triumph.

verses.summary: The largest difference in the psalm. {{10.9}} is a first person verb, I raise a shout, where Psalm 60:10 has a feminine imperative telling Philistia to shout, and the preposition before it here means over rather than over me.

stichs.en: Who will bring me to the fortified city?
Who has led me as far as Edom?

verses.summary: The confidence stops and the questions start, exactly as in Psalm 60:11. The noun at {{11.3}} is a different word for a fortified place than the one Psalm 60 uses, with the same sense.

stichs.en: Is it not You, God, who rejected us?
And You do not go out, God, with our armies.

verses.summary: Seven words where Psalm 60:12 has eight: the pronoun You that stands after {{12.0}} there is absent here, so the accusation is a touch less pointed.

stichs.en: Give us help against the foe,
for the rescue that people give is worthless.

verses.summary: Identical to Psalm 60:13. The whole request is one imperative, and the second line rules out every alternative source of help.

stichs.en: Through God we will do valiantly,
and He is the one who will trample our foes.

verses.summary: Identical to Psalm 60:14. The psalm ends on a first person plural after opening on a first person singular, so the private harp of verse 3 finishes as an army.

pardes.body: The plain fact about this psalm is its construction. Verse 1 is its own heading; verses 2 to 6 reproduce Psalm 57:8 to 12; verses 7 to 14 reproduce Psalm 60:7 to 14. Read as a single piece it has a shape neither parent has. Psalm 57 goes from danger to song, so its praise is an arrival. Psalm 60 goes from defeat to a request for help, so its plea is an ending. Psalm 108 puts the arrival first and then asks, which makes the questions of verses 11 and 12 land after the singer has already announced that God is exalted above the heavens. The seam is between verses 6 and 7, and it is audible: verse 6 is the last line of a refrain, verse 7 opens with a purpose word, so that the exaltation of verse 6 is retrospectively given a reason, that Your beloved may be rescued. Nothing was invented to join them. The join is the word at the start of verse 7 doing work it did not do in Psalm 60.

The differences from the parent psalms are small and worth counting, because they are the only places where this text is not simply quotation. Against Psalm 57: my heart is steady is said once instead of twice in verse 2, and the word my glory moves back from the next verse into this one, so that verse 3 loses one of its two imperatives to awake; the four letter name stands in verse 4 where Psalm 57 has my Lord, and the second verb of that verse gains a joining vav; verse 5 says the kindness is great above the heavens where Psalm 57 says as far as the heavens; verse 6 gains a vav on and over all the earth. Against Psalm 60: verse 9 loses the vav on the second mine; verse 11 uses one noun for a fortified city where Psalm 60 uses another; verse 12 lacks the pronoun You. There are also spelling differences that do not change a word, such as a vowel letter present in one text and absent in the other. The one difference that changes meaning is in verse 10: this psalm has a first person verb, over Philistia I raise a shout, while Psalm 60 has a feminine imperative addressed to Philistia herself. The direction of borrowing is disputed. The common view is that this psalm is the later compilation; it has also been argued that all three draw on older liturgical material, and the manuscripts settle neither.

A psalm made of two other psalms is a statement about how scripture was used, not only about how it was written. Two songs from named crises, a cave and a lost battle, are stripped of their headings and rejoined under three neutral words, and what was autobiography becomes something a congregation can say on any morning. The reuse also performs an argument. Placing the confidence of Psalm 57 before the complaint of Psalm 60 means the complaint is spoken by someone who has already sung, so the questions in verse 11 are not the questions of a man who has lost faith but of a man who has kept it and still has no army. Read that way, {{12.0}}, is it not, is the pivot of the whole compilation: praise does not exempt anyone from asking why the help has not come. The absence of the pronoun You in that verse, compared with the parent text, has been read as softening the charge, though a single missing word is thin ground for a doctrine.

The two halves can be read as two moments of the same movement rather than as two documents. The first half is upward: heart steady, instruments woken, the dawn woken after them, kindness measured above the heavens, glory over all the earth. The second half is downward and outward: the land parcelled out by name, the neighbouring kingdoms reduced to household objects, the armies, the foe. Between them stands the right hand of verse 7, which in kabbalistic idiom is the side of kindness and expansion, and it is asked to do the saving. On this reading the psalm is a description of how a thing sung in the small hours reaches the ground: it is woken privately at {{3.3}}, published among the nations in verse 4, raised above the heavens in verse 6, and only then applied to a specific map with specific enemies. Praise is not a mood here. It is the first stage of a descent into the world where the help is actually needed.
